newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GRAF FORGETS FATHER'S TROUBLES IN EASY WIN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF FORGETS FATHER'S TROUBLES IN EASY WIN.

text.p: Steffi Graf, making her first appearance on a tennis court in Germany since her father's tax evasion trial began last month, easily won her first match in the Leipzig tournament on Tuesday.
The world number one crushed American Kimberly Po, ranked 35th, 6-0 6-1 after having a first-round bye to move into the quarter-finals of the $450,000 tournament.

Graf's father, Peter, is accused of evading taxes on 19 million marks ($12.47 million) of his multimillionaire daughter's earnings between 1989 and 1993. He has been in detention since August last year and his trial began in Mannheim in September.
"I couldn't have played better, that was perfect tennis," Steffi Graf said after the 40-minute match with Po. "I am feeling very good at the moment. I don't have any injury problems."
Graf could face fellow German and titleholder Anke Huber in the semi-finals. Huber beat Ruxandra Dragomir of Romania 6-1 6-2.
"I am very satisified and played very aggressively," Huber said. "This victory was very good for my game. I haven't yet begun to think about a posssible duel against Steffi."
Graf, 27, said that her relationship with Huber, 21, has improved recently and the two had trained together regularly.
"I've trained with her quite a bit, even here in Leipzig and we've had a lot of fun," Graf said. "We have become friends."
Graf, who won the U.S. Open last month and who has captured the Leipzig title four times, has shown astonishing poise on court despite her father's legal troubles.
She has won 46 of her 49 matches and six of the eight tournaments she has entered this year. Her third defeat came in a Fed Cup tie.
Graf had last played in Germany in May, when she won a Berlin tournament.
Leipzig in eastern Germany is about 400 km east of the western city of Mannheim.
Peter Graf, who was known for collecting his daughter's winnings in cash in plastic bags, admits diverting money abroad out of the reach of German tax collectors.
But he says the authorities signalled their approval of his tax schemes on the basis that this would prevent Steffi joining an exodus of German sporting tax exiles.
